claims.sentence: NHS inform describes tension-type headache as the most common kind.
claims.evidence: Search for NHS inform headaches page did not return text ranking tension-type headache as most common; a search explicitly reported no source found.

claims.sentence: The NHS says tension headaches are not a sign of an underlying condition, and common triggers include stress, sleep problems and caffeine.
claims.evidence: NHS tension headaches page retrieved says treat with painkillers, see GP if several a week or severe, and you are normally well between headaches; no statement that it is not a sign of an underlying condition, and triggers list not retrieved.

claims.sentence: Migraine usually causes a moderate or severe throbbing pain, often on one side of the head.
claims.evidence: NHS migraine pages were returned but the throbbing/one-side wording was not in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: Other migraine symptoms include feeling sick and sensitivity to light and sound.
claims.evidence: Feeling sick and light/sound sensitivity not present in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: Some people also get an aura, such as seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights.
claims.evidence: NHS: about 1 in 3 people with migraine have aura; visual problems such as flashing lights, zig-zag patterns or blind spots are most common.

claims.sentence: NHS inform says migraine affects around 1 in 5 women and 1 in 15 men.
claims.evidence: NHS inform migraine: affects around 1 in 5 women and around 1 in 15 men.

claims.sentence: Cluster headaches are rare, and each attack is intensely painful, affects one side of the head and can happen several times a day.
claims.evidence: NHS inform describes cluster headaches as rare, in bouts of short daily headaches lasting a month or two, pain usually around the eye. 'Intensely painful', 'one side' and 'several times a day' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform describes cluster headaches as rare, coming in bouts of short daily headaches that last a month or two, with pain usually around the eye.

claims.sentence: Taking painkillers regularly can itself cause daily headaches, a problem called medication overuse headache.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text for medication overuse headache came from Great Ormond Street Hospital (develops and gets worse with frequent use of pain medicines, more than 15 days a month), not shown from NHS inform; 'daily' overstates.
claims.newSentence: Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain.

claims.sentence: NHS inform says it usually affects people who already have tension-type headaches or migraines.
claims.evidence: Only GOSH retrieved: occurs in people who have tension-type headache or migraine; not confirmed as NHS inform wording, and 'usually' not shown.
claims.newSentence: Great Ormond Street Hospital says medication overuse headache occurs in people who already have tension-type headache or migraine.

claims.sentence: Stopping the overused medicine usually helps, although the pain can get worse for a few days first.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: a Nottinghamshire NHS pathway says analgesic overuse headache improves or resolves within 3 months of stopping; other leaflets say worse for 2-10 days but URL not identified. NHS inform not shown.
claims.newSentence: A Nottinghamshire NHS pathway says headache from overusing painkillers improves or resolves within 3 months of stopping them.

claims.sentence: People who get headaches often and take painkillers regularly are advised to speak to a GP.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text advises frequent headaches plus regular painkillers should see a GP (NHS tension page: GP if several headaches a week or severe).

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury.
claims.evidence: NHS inform headaches: call 999 or go to A&E for headache that started suddenly and is very severe, or followed a severe head injury. Attribution is NHS inform; 'the NHS' acceptable but 'extremely painful' also echoed by NHS pages.

claims.sentence: Other reasons to call 999 include weakness on one side, slurred speech, trouble speaking or remembering, loss of vision, drowsiness, confusion, or a high temperature with a stiff neck or a rash that could mean meningitis.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: stroke signs (weakness one side of face/body, slurred speech), meningitis or sepsis signs, reduced alertness/drowsiness/confusion. Stiff neck, rash, high temperature, trouble remembering not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform lists other reasons to call 999 or go to A&E, including signs of stroke such as weakness on one side or slurred speech, signs of meningitis or sepsis, and being drowsy or confused.

claims.sentence: NHS inform lists headaches that wake someone at night, that are there on waking, that keep getting worse, or that are set off by coughing, sneezing or bending as reasons for an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111.
claims.evidence: NHS inform puts headache that wakes you from sleep or keeps getting worse despite treatment under contacting the GP practice (not urgent); only coughing/sneezing/posture/effort trigger is in the urgent tier (111 if practice closed). 'There on waking' and 'bending' not retrieved. Original merges tiers: route to care wrong.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform lists a headache set off by coughing, sneezing, a change in posture or effort as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. A headache that wakes someone from sleep, or keeps getting worse despite treatment, is listed under contacting the GP practice.

claims.sentence: A new headache in a person over 50, with a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing, can signal inflamed arteries and also needs urgent attention.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: sore scalp or jaw pain while chewing in someone over 50 is in the urgent GP tier (111 if closed). NHS cluster headache page links jaw pain on eating, sore scalp, blurred vision with temporal arteritis (urgent GP or 111). 'Inflamed arteries' not stated; 'new headache' only from a Nottinghamshire pathway.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform lists a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing in someone over 50 as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed.

claims.sentence: Headaches with vision changes, or with vomiting plus dizziness or weakness, also call for urgent review.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: changes in vision, or new/worsening headache with dizziness, vomiting or weakness, are urgent-GP tier (111 if closed). Original omitted the route, so edited to name it.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform lists changes in vision, or a new or worsening headache with dizziness, vomiting or weakness, as reasons to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed.

claims.sentence: An NHS formulary guideline describes giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, as a medical emergency that needs prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent permanent loss of vision.
claims.evidence: Buckinghamshire formulary guideline text: GCA is a medical emergency requiring prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent irreversible visual loss.

claims.sentence: An NHS trust page lists tiredness, loss of appetite, weight loss, fever and headache, with tenderness over the temples, jaw or tongue pain when eating, and blurred vision, as its symptoms.
claims.evidence: Royal Devon page was not returned this session. Symptom lists retrieved came from unidentified leaflets, so attribution cannot be verified.

claims.sentence: NHS pages describe triptans as a painkiller designed for migraine, which works by reversing the widening of blood vessels that is believed to be part of the migraine process.
claims.evidence: NHS migraine treatment: triptan is a painkiller made specifically for migraine, tablets, injections and nasal sprays. 'Reversing widening of blood vessels' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes triptans as a painkiller made specifically for migraine, available as tablets, injections and nasal sprays.

claims.sentence: If ordinary painkillers do not relieve migraine symptoms, the NHS advises making a GP appointment.
claims.evidence: The GP-appointment advice came from NHS inform (a GP may recommend a triptan if over-the-counter medicines are not helping), not the NHS England page, which said the painkiller dose may not be high enough. Original misattributes.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says a GP may recommend a triptan if over-the-counter medicines are not helping.

claims.sentence: Anti-sickness medicines can help during a migraine even without nausea, and the NHS says they work better when taken as soon as symptoms begin.
claims.evidence: NHS migraine treatment: anti-emetics can treat migraine in some people even without feeling sick; they work best taken early.

claims.sentence: An NHS-hosted leaflet advises against strong opioid painkillers such as codeine, tramadol and morphine for migraine because of the high risk of rebound headache.
claims.evidence: Leicester hospital leaflet URL was returned but its text was not retrieved; cannot verify opioid/rebound claim, and it is a hospital leaflet.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists common migraine triggers as stress, tiredness, lack of sleep, dehydration, missing meals, regular alcohol or caffeine, and foods such as cheese or chocolate, and suggests keeping a record to spot personal triggers.
claims.evidence: NHS.uk lists stress, tiredness, skipping meals and too much caffeine; cheese is not in the NHS.uk list (NHS inform lists chocolate/cheese-type foods); dehydration, alcohol, lack of sleep and 'keep a record' for triggers not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists stress, tiredness, skipping meals and too much caffeine among common migraine triggers.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP for tension headaches that happen several times a week, are severe, or do not respond to painkillers and relaxation.
claims.evidence: NHS tension headaches page: see a GP if you have several headaches a week or they're severe. 'Do not respond to painkillers and relaxation' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says tension headaches can be treated with painkillers, but advises seeing a GP for several headaches a week or severe ones.

claims.sentence: These can be signs of a different type of headache, such as migraine or cluster headache.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text says tension headache warning signs may be migraine or cluster headache.

claims.sentence: A GP may suggest keeping a headache diary that records how often the headaches happen and how long they last.
claims.evidence: NHS: a GP may suggest keeping a migraine diary. 'How often and how long' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A GP may suggest keeping a migraine diary.

claims.sentence: There is no specific test for migraine, so the GP looks for a pattern of recurring headaches with the typical symptoms.
claims.evidence: NHS: no specific test to diagnose migraine; GP identifies a pattern of recurring headaches with the associated symptoms.

claims.sentence: Simple painkillers, rest and fluids are the first step for most headaches.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved from NHS inform; regional ICB guidance mentions simple analgesia for less frequent tension headache only. Also reads as advice.

claims.sentence: If painkillers and exercise do not help, a person may be referred to a specialist, and a medicine called amitriptyline may be offered to help prevent tension headaches.
claims.evidence: NHS tension page: amitriptyline sometimes recommended to help prevent tension headaches; usually taken for several months before it works. Referral to a specialist not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says an antidepressant medicine called amitriptyline is sometimes recommended to help prevent tension headaches.

claims.sentence: Most headaches are tension-type headaches or migraines, but a sudden, extremely painful headache needs a 999 call.
claims.evidence: 'Most headaches are tension-type or migraine' not retrieved. Emergency part is supported by NHS inform (999 or A&E for sudden, very severe headache).
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that starts suddenly and is very severe.

notes: Retrieval was thin: summaries often did not quote the NHS pages, so many sentences are unsupported for lack of retrieved text rather than shown false. Key: NHS inform puts night-waking headache in the non-urgent GP tier, not urgent (c14). Medication overuse and GCA symptom claims were attributed to NHS inform or a trust page not actually retrieved. Blank url means no returned URL carried the claim. Removing c01-c04, c11 leaves the body without a plain definition of tension headache or migraine symptoms; a re-search with exact NHS page titles could restore them. NHS inform is Scottish (NHS 24 / 111 routes); site is UK so keep route wording consistent.
